ai.definition: 2D materials beyond graphene refer to a class of two-dimensional crystalline materials with distinct physical and chemical properties that differ from those of graphene. These materials include molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂), tungsten diselenide (WSe₂), and others, each offering unique characteristics such as high electron mobility, optical transparency, or catalytic activity.
ai.howItWorks: These materials can be integrated into electronic devices by depositing them onto substrates using techniques like chemical vapor deposition (CVD) or mechanical exfoliation. Their properties allow for the creation of thin, flexible electronics and sensors with enhanced performance compared to traditional materials.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional materials often have limitations in terms of flexibility, conductivity, or energy storage capacity. 2D materials beyond graphene offer solutions by providing higher electron mobility, better optical properties, and improved catalytic efficiency, among other benefits.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing these materials involves advanced techniques such as CVD, atomic layer deposition (ALD), and exfoliation from bulk crystals to produce thin layers. These processes require precise control over temperature, pressure, and chemical reactions.
ai.buildProcess: The build process typically includes the synthesis of precursor materials, followed by their transformation into 2D structures through controlled growth or exfoliation methods. The resulting films are then transferred onto substrates for integration into devices.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of manufacturing processes, the need for high-purity starting materials, and the requirement for specialized equipment. Scalability is a significant challenge that affects overall cost.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for these materials is promising but faces several hurdles before widespread commercial adoption. They are currently in early-stage development with limited industrial applications.
ai.regulation: Current regulations are not specific to 2D materials beyond graphene, so they follow general guidelines for nanomaterials and chemical substances. However, as these materials gain more traction, specialized regulations may be developed.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include potential toxicity if not properly handled during production and disposal. Health risks could arise from inhalation or skin contact with nanoparticles. Technological risks involve the need for new manufacturing processes and integration into existing systems.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the high research costs and limited market penetration. However, successful commercialization could lead to significant financial gains in specific sectors such as electronics and energy storage.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving synthesis methods, reducing production costs, and expanding applications across various industries. Collaboration between academia and industry is crucial for advancing this field.

glossary.def: Materials with a thickness of only one or a few atomic layers, offering unique physical and chemical properties.
A process used to deposit thin films by the reaction of gaseous precursors on a substrate at elevated temperatures.
A technique for growing thin films that involves sequential surface reactions with gas precursors, providing precise control over film thickness and composition.

subsystems.name: Monolayer crystal
subsystems.role: the active material itself, one to a few atoms thick, with properties that bulk versions do not have.

subsystems.name: Growth template
subsystems.role: the surface or catalyst that templates the crystal as it forms.

subsystems.name: Transfer medium
subsystems.role: lifts a delicate monolayer off its growth substrate and onto the device wafer without tearing it.

subsystems.name: Device stack
subsystems.role: turns the bare material into a working electronic or optical component.

subsystems.name: Heterostructure assembly
subsystems.role: stacks different 2D layers so their interfaces produce behaviour no single layer has.

subsystems.name: Characterisation
subsystems.role: measures thickness, defects and electronic quality, which are hard to see in a single atomic layer.

buildSteps.title: Choose the material for the job
buildSteps.detail: Semiconducting, insulating or metallic 2D crystals are picked depending on whether the device needs to switch current, block it or conduct it.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the monolayer
buildSteps.detail: Research often starts with mechanical exfoliation — peeling flakes off a crystal with tape — while scale-up uses chemical vapour deposition or metal-organic CVD to grow films on a wafer.

buildSteps.title: Transfer to the target wafer
buildSteps.detail: If the growth substrate is not the final one, a polymer film is coated over the monolayer, the underlying template is etched away, and the film is laid down and dissolved off.

buildSteps.title: Pattern the film
buildSteps.detail: Lithography and etching cut the monolayer into the shapes needed for transistors, sensors or memory cells.

buildSteps.title: Deposit contacts and dielectric
buildSteps.detail: Metals are evaporated or deposited to form electrodes, and an insulating layer is grown on top to gate the channel.

buildSteps.title: Stack additional layers
buildSteps.detail: Extra 2D layers are aligned and pressed on top so the device becomes a heterostructure, for example a semiconductor sandwiched between two insulators.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate
buildSteps.detail: A protective layer seals the stack, because a single atomic layer oxidises or absorbs moisture quickly in air.

buildSteps.title: Test and iterate
buildSteps.detail: Electrical and optical measurements reveal whether the material survived the process; failures usually send the wafer back to the growth or transfer stage.

prerequisites.why: growing one perfect flake is routine, but growing a uniform film across a 200 or 300 mm wafer is not.
moving a monolayer from its growth substrate to a device wafer often introduces tears, wrinkles and polymer residue.
metal-to-2D junctions have high resistance, which limits how fast and efficient devices can be.

prerequisites.tech: Uniform high-k dielectrics on inert surfaces
prerequisites.why: atomic layer deposition needs chemical handles that 2D surfaces lack, so the insulator often grows unevenly.
you cannot fix what you cannot see, and defects in a monolayer are hard to count reliably at scale.

pathway.milestone: exfoliated and CVD-grown flakes used in research transistors, sensors and photodetectors
pathway.unlocks: proof that single-layer materials can outperform bulk ones in specific roles.

pathway.milestone: wafer-scale growth of transition metal dichalcogenides and hexagonal boron nitride
pathway.unlocks: pilot production of 2D sensors, memory selectors and flexible electronics.

pathway.milestone: back-end-of-line integration in silicon fabs, stacking 2D devices above conventional logic
pathway.unlocks: more function per chip without shrinking silicon transistors further.

pathway.milestone: 2D channel transistors and dense 3D memory in commercial products
pathway.unlocks: continued scaling and new device types once silicon reaches its limits.
